column1: # The grove's art, and where each piece came from.
# One row per piece. `import_grove_art.py` copies the source PNG to
# Assets/Game/Art/Homestead/<id>.png, writes the loc string, and regenerates the
# `pieces` array of homestead.json from this file.
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. A piece id is written into save files, so it is permanent
# (invariant 1) — and the art behind it is not, because packs get re-cut and
# replaced. Keeping the mapping here means the id, the price and the source path
# are reviewed together in a diff, an import can be re-run without hand-copying
# anything, and the day a real village pack lands the change is one column.
# WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. The 17 downloaded packs hold 1,056 files, 936 of
# them distinct — but they are one series, so the same signpost, skull, ladder and
# stone ship in nearly all of them. Deduplicated by content and then by *object*,
# 936 files reduce to roughly 120 distinct things you could stand on an island, and
# the 124 rows below are those. What is excluded is 249 numbered level tiles and
# platform chips, the UI furniture (hearts, progress bars, map pins, coin piles,
# gift boxes, reward stars) and the packs' mascot avatars. Importing those would
# put 900 sprites in the bundle to sell a player a progress bar.
# columns: source (relative to the pack root) | id | slot | cost | bundle | scale | lift | name
# BUNDLE is how many copies one purchase grants (see HomesteadPiece.Bundle).
# The four scatter kinds — ground, bed, edge, path — sell in tens at the price
# a single one used to cost, because a grove wants a dozen fences and buying
# them one tap at a time is a chore rather than a decision. Trees and
# structures sell singly: you want a handful and one well. A price must be
# divisible by its bundle, so that a copy is worth exactly cost/bundle and a
# grove's worth is the credits that were actually paid for it.
